preamble: First half of the Arabic development of the Proto-Semitic emphatic lateral. *ṣ́, reconstructed as an ejective lateral fricative [ɬʼ], is Arabic ḍād ض, which in Classical Arabic was still a voiced lateral. Sibawayh placed it at 'the beginning of the edge of the tongue and the adjoining molars' and called it majhūr ('unbreathed'), rakhw ('lax') and muṭbaq ('lidded, emphatic') (trans. Dickins 1990: 237, quoted by Watson & Al-Azraqi 2011: 426). It is reconstructed as pharyngealized [ɮˤ] or an affricate [d͡ɮˤ] (Versteegh 1999, 2000, cited by Wikipedia); Cantineau (1960) read the description as a lateral or lateralized velarized voiced interdental fricative (per Watson & Al-Azraqi 2011: 426), and André Roman proposed [ʑˤ] instead (Wikipedia, Ḍād). Spanish alcalde < qāḍī and aldea < aḍ-ḍayʕa show the lateral in loans (Watson & Al-Azraqi 2011: 426). Between the two ends, glottalization gives way to pharyngealization and the lateral fricative is voiced. Wiktionary describes [ɮˤ] as the 'widely considered' value of the letter around 700 AD, so that end is also a reconstruction. Lateral reflexes of ḍād survive in the Saudi Tihāmah and Asir: Asiri (2009, cited by Watson & Al-Azraqi 2011: 428) describes the Rijal Almaʿ reflex as a voiced lateralized pharyngealized interdental fricative, transcribed ḏ̣ˡ, and the younger generation of al-Rubūʕah has the same type. The Mehri of Hawf has a voiced lateralized pharyngealized fricative with less friction, as in ḏ̣ˡōfar 'plait' (Watson & Al-Azraqi 2011: 429). The Proto-Semitic value is itself a reconstruction: the emphatics are generally reconstructed as glottalized (Cantineau 1952; Kogan 2011: 61, cited by Wikipedia), and 'maximal' accounts make *ṣ́ an affricate [tɬʼ] (Wikipedia, Proto-Semitic language). This entry follows the [ɬʼ] of Wikipedia's Proto-Semitic consonant table.

examples.to: Classical Arabic أَرْض ʔarḍ 'earth, land', with lateral ḍ
Classical Arabic مَرِضَ mariḍa 'to be sick', with lateral ḍ
examples.note: Mehri mērəẑ, Jibbali mírẓ̂, Harsusi mēreẑ (Wiktionary).

examples.to: Classical Arabic ضَأْن ḍaʔn 'sheep' (collective), with lateral ḍ
Classical Arabic ضَرَّة ḍarra 'co-wife', with lateral ḍ
Classical Arabic ضَرَطَ ḍaraṭa 'to fart', with lateral ḍ
examples.note: Mehri ẑərūṭ, Jibbali ẓ̂érɔ́ṭ, Harsusi ẑerōṭ (Wiktionary).

Asiri (2009), cited by Watson & Al-Azraqi (2011: 428). ḏ̣ˡ is a voiced lateralized pharyngealized interdental fricative, so [ɮˤ] is approximate. Watson & Al-Azraqi add that the correspondence is not always clean: ḏ̣ˡarf 'circumstance' has this sound although it continues *ẓarf (Asiri 2009, cited by Watson & Al-Azraqi 2011: 428).
Minimal pair with ṯ̣ˡaym 'has been affected', which has the voiceless reflex of *ẓ (Watson & Al-Azraqi 2011: 428).
